Comparer.meta_desc: Compare the total cost of ownership (TCO) of all powertrains for your segment: diesel, electric, hydrogen, NGV, PHEV, e-fuel. Incentives, energy and maintenance included.
Comparer.lead: All powertrains side by side — net purchase, energy, maintenance, incentives included. Adjust your inputs and the table recalculates instantly.
Comparer.faq_q1: What's the difference between the TCO comparator and the simulator?
Comparer.faq_a1: The TCO comparator is designed for a side-by-side synthetic view of all powertrains in your segment: it ranks results from cheapest to most expensive and highlights the winner. The custom simulator offers more parameters (per-powertrain purchase price, discounts, detailed usage profile). Use the comparator to decide quickly, then the simulator to fine-tune.
Comparer.faq_q2: Is electric really cheaper than diesel over 4 years?
Comparer.faq_a2: In most B2B scenarios in France in 2026 (medium van, 25,000 km/year), yes: the eco-bonus + low charging cost bring electric TCO below diesel. But the result depends on mileage, usage (motorway vs urban), country and available incentives. Adjust the parameters in the comparator to test your real situation.
Comparer.faq_a3: Maintenance costs are estimated from 2026 industry averages by segment (LCV, truck, etc.) and powertrain. Electric is cheaper (no oil change, no clutch, brakes less worn thanks to regenerative braking). Diesel and petrol include oil changes, filters and timing belts. PHEVs combine both. These values are adjusted by the annual mileage entered.
Comparer.faq_q4: Is NGV (natural gas) relevant for my fleet?
Comparer.faq_a4: NGV (and its biogas equivalent, bioCNG) is particularly competitive for high mileage (> 50,000 km/year) and heavy trucks in France, thanks to a growing station network and a lower fuel cost than diesel. For small or medium LCVs with short trips, electric is usually more advantageous. The comparator lets you see both side by side.
Comparer.faq_q5: Are incentives and subsidies factored in?
Comparer.faq_a5: Yes. The comparator automatically applies 2026 incentives based on the selected country: eco-bonus (France), full BEV tax deductibility (Belgium), cantonal exemptions (Switzerland) and the iZEV programme (Canada). The displayed purchase price is the net price after incentives.
Comparer.faq_q6: How should I read the « winner » badge?
Comparer.faq_a6: The 🏆 badge is given to the powertrain whose total TCO is the lowest over the selected duration, for the inputs entered. It doesn't mean this powertrain is the best in every case: a range constraint, the absence of a charging station on site, or a limited distribution network can make another option more suitable for your situation.

ComparerTrajet.ped_h2: What this comparator takes into account

ComparerTrajet.ped_3_desc: Number of stops calculated based on real motorway range (~270 km). Charging duration added to trip time.

ComparerTrajet.seo_lead: Cost by powertrain, vignettes, LEZ, charging and checklist for the most popular European routes.
ComparerTrajet.cta_intro: Thinking of changing vehicle? Go further:
ComparerTrajet.faq_q1: How is the motorway charging cost calculated?
ComparerTrajet.faq_a1: The comparator uses the fast charging rate (DC ≥ 50 kW) at public motorway stations, roughly €0.55-0.65/kWh in France in 2026. This rate is significantly higher than home charging (~€0.20/kWh). If you have an operator subscription or mainly charge at home before leaving, the actual cost can be lower. Change the country to adapt rates.
ComparerTrajet.faq_q2: How many charging stops are needed Paris-Marseille in electric?
ComparerTrajet.faq_a2: For a trip of roughly 780 km, with a realistic motorway range of about 270 km, 2 to 3 charging stops are needed depending on starting charge level. The comparator automatically calculates the number of stops and adds charging time (~25 min per fast-charging stop) to the total trip duration.
ComparerTrajet.faq_q3: Are tolls included in the total cost?
ComparerTrajet.faq_a3: Yes, for the 25 pre-filled trips, toll amounts are integrated into the total cost (standard 2026 rate, without electronic toll subscription). Tolls apply equally to all powertrains, so they only affect the ranking if a powertrain benefits from a partial or full exemption (some European tolls exempt EVs).
ComparerTrajet.faq_q4: Is a PHEV (plug-in hybrid) really advantageous on motorways?
ComparerTrajet.faq_a4: On motorways, PHEVs quickly lose their electric advantage: after about 50 km, the thermal engine takes over with consumption often higher than an equivalent diesel (5-7 L/100 km). The PHEV advantage is mostly visible on mixed trips (city + road). The comparator models this honestly: the first 50 km electric, then thermal.
ComparerTrajet.faq_q5: Can I enter a trip not in the list?
ComparerTrajet.faq_a5: Yes. In addition to the 25 pre-filled popular trips, you can freely enter a departure and arrival address. The comparator geocodes the addresses, calculates the real distance via the OpenRouteService API and estimates costs. The distance is an estimate (recommended road itinerary) and tolls are approximated for free trips.
ComparerTrajet.faq_q6: Are energy prices up to date?
ComparerTrajet.faq_a6: Prices are regularly updated by the Moteurs.com Simulator Agent from official sources (DGEC France, European Commission). They reflect 2026 national averages for petrol, diesel, electricity (public fast charging) and NGV. Real prices may vary by retailer and region.

Simulateur.meta_desc: Simulate the total cost of ownership (purchase + energy + maintenance + incentives) across 6 powertrains.
Simulateur.lead: Calculate the total cost of ownership (purchase + energy + maintenance + incentives) across 6 powertrains. All parameters are editable, all assumptions are displayed.
Simulateur.embed_note: The interactive tool below is currently available in French only — field labels (Country, Segment, Mileage…) remain in French. Form translation is scheduled in an upcoming wave.
Simulateur.disclaimer: Disclaimer — This simulator produces an indicative estimate based on 2026 averages. Real amounts (purchase, incentives, energy, maintenance) vary by operator, dealer and your eligibility. Check your situation with a professional before any commitment. Moteurs.com is not a financial advisor.
Simulateur.faq_q1: What is TCO (total cost of ownership)?
Simulateur.faq_a1: TCO (Total Cost of Ownership) is the real cost of a vehicle over its entire use period: net purchase price after incentives, fuel or electricity, maintenance, insurance and taxation. Unlike the simple purchase price, TCO lets you objectively compare all powertrains on the same basis.
Simulateur.faq_q2: Which powertrain is cheapest over 4 years in France?
Simulateur.faq_a2: For a medium B2B van running 25,000 km/year in France, the electric vehicle is generally the cheapest over 4 years thanks to incentives (eco-bonus, regional aids) and low energy cost. NGV often comes second for high mileages. Diesel remains competitive for fleets that charge little or mainly drive on motorways. Adjust the simulator parameters to get the result specific to your situation.
Simulateur.faq_q3: Are government incentives included in the calculation?
Simulateur.faq_a3: Yes. The simulator includes the main 2026 incentives for France (eco-bonus, weight malus), Belgium (100% BEV deductibility), Switzerland (cantonal exemptions) and Canada (federal iZEV programme). Incentives are applied automatically based on the selected country and segment. Always check your eligibility with a professional before any commitment.
Simulateur.faq_q4: How do I change the purchase price in the simulator?
Simulateur.faq_a4: In the left column, the « Real purchase price » section lets you enter the price after dealer discount for each powertrain. You can also apply a uniform global discount (in euros) added to individual prices. If you leave the fields empty, the simulator uses the 2026 catalogue reference prices.
Simulateur.faq_q5: Does the simulator work for Belgium, Switzerland and Canada?
Simulateur.faq_a5: Yes. Select the country from the drop-down menu: energy prices, tax incentives and VAT adapt automatically. Data is regularly updated by the Moteurs.com Simulator Agent from official sources (DGEC, European Commission).
Simulateur.faq_q6: What does « driving profile » mean and why does it matter?
Simulateur.faq_a6: The driving profile (urban, mixed, road, motorway) directly affects consumption. An electric vehicle consumes much less in town than on the motorway, while it's the opposite for diesel. For LCVs, the « mixed » profile is most representative of a typical delivery use. Adjust according to your real-world use to get the most accurate estimate.

HubRecharge.meta_desc: EV charging prices by country (France, Belgium, Switzerland, Canada), home vs public, AC/DC stations, charging cards, installation, incentives. Everything to optimise charging cost in {annee}.
HubRecharge.og_desc: Prices, stations, cards, installation, incentives — everything on EV charging.
HubRecharge.hero_lead: Everything you need to know to charge your electric car in {annee}: how much it costs by country and charging mode, which station to install at home, which card to choose for trips, which incentives to claim. Data verified and updated monthly by our Simulator Agent.
HubRecharge.tarif_h2: How much does 1 kWh of charging cost in {annee}?
HubRecharge.tarif_note: Reference residential rates (peak hours / average rate). A full 60 kWh charge (~350 km range) costs on average €{moyenne} in Europe. On public fast charging (DC), expect 2 to 3 times more.
HubRecharge.domvspub_h2: Charge at home or on the public network?
HubRecharge.domvspub_rule_body: 80% of your charging should happen at home (or work). Public fast stations are 2-3x more expensive and accelerate battery wear; reserve them for long trips.
HubRecharge.cards_body: In Europe, over 25 charging cards share the market: IONITY Motion, Chargemap, Plugsurfing, Shell Recharge, Izivia, Electra, Fastned, etc. Our comparators detail the prices by country for each.
HubRecharge.autoroute_body: On the main European routes, the density of fast DC stations is now sufficient for any holiday trip. Our trip pages automatically calculate the number of stops needed based on your vehicle's range (270 km real motorway average).
HubRecharge.autoroute_trip_label: Trip in electric — stops & charging cost
HubRecharge.install_card1_body: Wall-box 7.4 kW or 11 kW: €800-2,500 installation included. No authorisation needed if you are the owner. FR tax credit of €500 on installation in {annee}.
HubRecharge.install_card2_body: Right-to-plug: any co-owner can have a station installed on their space. The building cannot oppose it (LOM law in France). Advenir bonus up to €960.
HubRecharge.install_card2_link: → Complete guide to charging in apartment buildings
HubRecharge.install_card3_body: 40% accelerated depreciation in France for on-site stations (until end {annee}). Advenir B2B bonus up to €2,100 per public-accessible charging point.
HubRecharge.aides_fr: France — €500 tax credit per station (individuals), Advenir B2B bonus up to €2,100, reduced 5.5% VAT for pro installation.
HubRecharge.aides_be: Belgium — 30-45% tax deduction on installation up to €3,750 (Wallonia + Flanders), varies by region.
HubRecharge.aides_ch: Switzerland — Mixed cantonal subsidies (Vaud, Geneva active) — up to CHF 1,500 per station.
HubRecharge.aides_ca: Canada — iZEV federal programme + QC/BC provincial credits for residential stations (up to CAD 600).
HubRecharge.faq_title: Frequently asked questions on EV charging
HubRecharge.faq_q1: How much does a full home charge cost in 2026?
HubRecharge.faq_a1: For a 60 kWh battery (WLTP range ~350 km), expect about €11 in France at regulated peak rate (€0.21/kWh), €7.80 if you have off-peak rate (€0.13/kWh). In Belgium: ~€18. In Switzerland: ~€16. A full home charge remains 2 to 3 times cheaper than a public fast charge.
HubRecharge.faq_q2: What station power should I install at home?
HubRecharge.faq_a2: For daily use (50-80 km/day), a 7.4 kW station (single-phase) is largely sufficient and charges about 40 km per hour. If you drive a lot or have three-phase wiring, opt for 11 kW (60 km/h). 22 kW is rarely useful for an individual — most cars are limited to 11 kW in AC.
HubRecharge.faq_q3: Should I subscribe to a charging operator?
HubRecharge.faq_a3: If you mainly charge at home (≥ 80% of the time) and do a few long trips per year: a no-subscription card like Chargemap Pass or Shell Recharge is enough. If you drive +20,000 km/year with regular fast-station use: a subscription (IONITY Motion, Fastned Gold, Electra) can reduce cost/kWh by 30-50%. Our comparator shows the break-even point.
HubRecharge.faq_q4: Is real range close to WLTP?
HubRecharge.faq_a4: No. In real mixed cycle, expect 80-85% of WLTP (350 km advertised = 280-300 km in practice). On motorway at 130 km/h: 60-70% of WLTP (350 km = 210-245 km). In winter at -5°C: 70-75% of WLTP. The most efficient cars on motorways in 2026: Tesla Model 3, Hyundai Ioniq 6, Mercedes EQE.
HubRecharge.faq_q5: Can I install a station in an apartment building without general meeting approval?
HubRecharge.faq_a5: In France, the « right-to-plug » (LOM law 2019) allows any co-owner to install a station on their space, at their expense, without general assembly approval. The management must be informed. The Advenir bonus covers up to €960 of installation. In Belgium and Switzerland, similar schemes exist. See our detailed apartment-building charging guide.
HubRecharge.faq_q6: Charging on motorways during holidays: how many stops?
HubRecharge.faq_a6: For a car with ~60 kWh battery (Tesla Model Y, Kia EV6, VW ID.4) and 270 km real motorway range, expect 1 stop every ~200 km of continuous driving (charge 20 → 80% in 25-30 min on 150 kW station). On Paris-Nice (930 km): 2-3 stops. Our trip comparator calculates the detail for each major European route.
HubRecharge.faq_q7: What tax incentive for the station in France in 2026?
HubRecharge.faq_a7: For individuals: flat €500 tax credit per station installed by IRVE pro. For businesses: 40% accelerated depreciation (additional tax deduction) on station price, until end 2026. For public-accessible stations (business parking lots, shops): Advenir B2B bonus of €1,000 to €2,100 depending on power.

HubVacances.faq_q1: What's the best day to leave for car holidays in 2026?
HubVacances.faq_a1: To avoid traffic in France, leave on a Sunday morning early (before 5am) or a Tuesday mid-afternoon. Avoid Saturdays classified red or black by Bison Futé (August 1st and 8th especially). Evening departures (after 8pm) also work well if your children can sleep in the car.
HubVacances.faq_q2: What's the average cost of a car holiday trip?
HubVacances.faq_a2: For a 1,200 km trip (national average), count €130-180 in fuel for diesel/petrol, plus €60-120 in tolls depending on route, so €200-300 round trip. In electric, fuel drops to €50-80 with mixed home/motorway charging, so €110-180 round trip with tolls. Our trip comparator calculates the exact cost for your vehicle.
HubVacances.faq_q3: Which vignettes to buy to cross Europe by car?
HubVacances.faq_a3: Four countries require a motorway vignette: Switzerland (CHF 40 annual), Austria (€12.40 for 10 days), Slovenia (€16 for 7 days), Czech Republic. Croatia and Hungary use classic tolls. Buy vignettes online before departure — the fine without a vignette is €200-800 depending on country.
HubVacances.faq_q4: Can you take a long holiday trip by electric car without issues?
HubVacances.faq_a4: Yes, without difficulty in 2026 on the main European routes. A modern electric car (Tesla, Kia EV6, Hyundai Ioniq 5, VW ID.4) with a 60-80 kWh battery allows 250-280 km at 130 km/h, then 25-30 minutes of fast DC charging. On Paris-Nice (930 km), count 2-3 stops i.e. 1h30 of charging breaks — often similar to what a family would do anyway.
HubVacances.faq_q5: How to avoid tolls in France for holidays?
HubVacances.faq_a5: Enable the « avoid tolls » option in Waze or Google Maps. Savings: €60-150 on a long trip. Cost: 1-2 hours additional and less comfort (national roads, town crossings, roundabouts). Smart mixed strategy: motorway in the morning for long stretches, national roads in the afternoon for scenery and breaks.
HubVacances.faq_q6: Do you need a specific European insurance claim form?
HubVacances.faq_a6: The European insurance claim form is multilingual and valid in all EU countries. You can download it for free, fill it out in advance with your details, and slide it into the glove box. Our claim tool offers a guided wizard in 8 steps, with PDF export and email sending — you save 20 minutes in case of accident.
HubVacances.faq_q7: What mandatory equipment in the car to cross Europe?
HubVacances.faq_a7: The minimum everywhere: warning triangle, fluorescent vest (1 per person in France, otherwise 1 minimum), first-aid kit (mandatory in Germany and Austria), driving licence, registration certificate, insurance certificate. In mountains (Mountain law France, Italy, Austria): snow chains or winter tyres are mandatory from October/November to April depending on country.

HubDepannage.etapes_h2: What to do step by step in case of breakdown?
HubDepannage.etapes_1_body: turn on hazard lights, exit on the side opposite traffic, put on your reflective vest before getting out, place the warning triangle 30 m behind (150 m on motorway).
HubDepannage.etapes_2_body: go behind the safety barrier, NEVER stay in the vehicle on the hard shoulder.
HubDepannage.etapes_3_body_a: Red warning light? Abnormal noise? Smoke? Our

HubDepannage.assur_h2: Do you have assistance in your insurance?
HubDepannage.assur_intro: Most car insurance includes basic assistance (« 0 km breakdown » or « beyond 50 km from home »). Check your contract before a long trip.
HubDepannage.assur_card1_body: Covers any breakdown, even in front of your home. The most complete. Often optional (+€30-80/year) or included in comprehensive policies.
HubDepannage.assur_card2_body: Standard: only covers breakdown if you are more than 50 km from home. Sufficient for holidays, but not daily life.
HubDepannage.assur_card3_body: Includes replacement vehicle, hotel, passenger repatriation, taxi. Consider for long family trips or company vehicles.
HubDepannage.faq_q1: What to do if I break down on a motorway?
HubDepannage.faq_a1: 1) Turn on hazard lights and try to reach the hard shoulder (HS). 2) Exit on the side opposite traffic, put on your reflective vest BEFORE getting out. 3) Place the warning triangle 150 m behind, ideally after a bend. 4) Go behind the safety barrier. 5) Call breakdown via the orange terminal every 2 km — fastest way. NEVER stay in the vehicle on the HS.
HubDepannage.faq_q2: My engine light is on: can I drive?
HubDepannage.faq_a2: It depends on colour and flashing. Steady orange: drive carefully to your usual garage, get diagnosed soon (often a sensor). Flashing orange: slow down immediately, potentially serious fault (ignition, injection). Red: STOP as soon as safely possible, engine risks damage. Our photo warning light scan diagnoses precisely in 30 seconds.
HubDepannage.faq_q3: How much does a classic breakdown cost in 2026?
HubDepannage.faq_a3: On open road (excluding motorway): €80-200 for a simple on-site call-out (battery, puncture). If towing to garage needed: €150-350. On motorways, prices are regulated in France: about €150 weekdays, €215 nights or Sundays, per 10 km of towing. Your insurance assistance generally covers all or part.
HubDepannage.faq_a4: Yes — 112 is the single European emergency number, valid in 27 EU countries plus Iceland, Norway, Switzerland, UK. It works free of charge, without credit, and even without a SIM card in some cases. Operators speak at least English. For mechanical breakdown only (no injured), prefer national numbers: 112 in CH/IT/ES/BE, or your insurance number.
HubDepannage.faq_q5: How to fill an insurance claim form abroad?
HubDepannage.faq_a5: The European insurance claim form is multilingual and standardised: fill it in your language, the other driver in theirs, the boxes match exactly. Our insurance claim tool offers an 8-step guided wizard covering the 17 standard cases and 10 European impact points. PDF export ready to print + email to both parties.
HubDepannage.faq_q6: My insurance refuses to cover the breakdown — what to do?
HubDepannage.faq_a6: First check covered mileage (« 0 km » vs « +50 km from home »), any excess, and exclusions (running out of fuel, neglected maintenance). In case of unjustified refusal, ask for written reason, dispute with customer service, then with the insurance ombudsman (free). Last resort: the ACPR or a lawyer (covered by your legal protection if any).
HubDepannage.faq_q7: How to avoid breakdowns on long trips?
HubDepannage.faq_a7: A service before departure is the best investment (€80-150). Essential checks: tyre pressure (cold, with real load), levels (oil, coolant, washer fluid), lights and indicators, battery (free test at auto centre), wipers. Fill up the day before to avoid leaving on empty. And check our departure checklist.

HubCout.faq_a1: TCO (Total Cost of Ownership) is the total ownership cost of a vehicle over its holding period. It adds purchase price (or lease), fuel or electricity, maintenance, insurance, depreciation, tolls and taxation. It's the most honest indicator for comparing two different powertrains: an EV more expensive to buy is often cheaper in TCO thanks to reduced energy and maintenance.
HubCout.faq_q2: Which powertrain is cheapest over 5 years in France?
HubCout.faq_a2: For average private use (15,000 km/year), three typical cases: 1) long motorway trips + public charging: diesel remains competitive; 2) mixed trips + home charging: electric is unbeatable (savings of €3,000 to €6,000 over 5 years vs diesel); 3) short trips < 80 km/day: electric with home charging = lowest TCO by far. Our simulator calculates your precise case.
HubCout.faq_q3: Is an electric car really more expensive to buy?
HubCout.faq_a3: Yes new: count +€5,000 to +€10,000 vs an equivalent thermal of same range. But after eco-bonus (€4,000 in 2026), scrappage scheme and B2B exempt company car tax, the purchase gap reduces to €1,000-3,000. Over 5 years with home charging, this premium is recovered in energy + maintenance. Second-hand, 2-3 year-old EVs are often the best deals on the market.
HubCout.faq_q4: How much does maintaining an electric vs diesel car cost?
HubCout.faq_a4: An EV costs about half in maintenance: €400-600/year vs €900-1,200/year for diesel. Reasons: no oil change, no oil filter, no timing belt, less worn brakes (regeneration). Remains: tyres (more expensive special compound), battery coolant every 4 years, brake/suspension check. Over 5 years, maintenance savings exceed €2,500.
HubCout.faq_q5: Does depreciation kill the electric advantage?
HubCout.faq_a5: Not in 2026. Until 2023, EVs effectively depreciated 5-10 points more than thermals (obsolete range, battery fear). Since 2024, the EV second-hand market is mature: 2022-2024 models depreciate at a normal pace (40-50% in 4 years, like equivalent diesel). Tesla Model 3/Y, Kia EV6, Hyundai Ioniq 5 have the best ratings.
HubCout.faq_q6: How to reduce my car's total cost?
HubCout.faq_a6: Five major levers: 1) buy in lease to spread depreciation (but pay more in interest); 2) optimise fuel (toll badge, cheapest fuel app); 3) maintenance at independent or secondary network (-30% vs dealership); 4) insurance comparator (change every 2 years, ~€200/year gain); 5) maximise incentives (bonus, scrappage, B2B accelerated depreciation). Our simulator integrates all these parameters.
HubCout.faq_q7: What exactly is the 40% accelerated depreciation in France?
HubCout.faq_a7: It's an additional tax deduction for companies buying an electric, hydrogen or NGV commercial vehicle. It adds to classic depreciation: 40% of the vehicle's pre-tax price (capped at €60,000 by segment) is deducted from taxable result. Concretely, for an electric LCV at €32,000 excl. tax: tax savings of €3,200 (at 25% corporate tax). Mechanism extended until end 2026.
